chunks: Basic grounding layout techniques. The question: Describe some basic grounding layout techniques.
Basic grounding techniques are layout moves that give every return current a short, well-defined, low-inductance path. Use a solid ground plane under the signals.
Connect each ground pad to the plane with a via right at the pad. Keep decoupling capacitor loops as small as you can. Keep noisy and sensitive circuits apart by placement.
Each move shrinks a loop or stops two circuits sharing one.
Picture an emergency exit. A door beside the room lets people out quickly. One at the end of a long corridor delays them.
A ground via touching the pad is the door beside the room.
A ground connection that first runs several millimeters of trace is the long corridor, and each millimeter adds about a nanohenry.
The analogy breaks in one place: you must build the short path on purpose, because the current has no other way out.
Same capacitor and plane, two connections. On the left the via touches the capacitor pad and goes straight to the adjacent plane: tiny loop.
On the right the ground leg runs several millimetres to a via, adding trace inductance (about 1 nanohenries/mm) to the loop.
Via: a plated hole that connects layers. A short one to the nearest plane has very little inductance. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current, in nanohenries (nH).
A current step through it makes a voltage spike.
Decoupling loop: the path from a capacitor to the chip pin and back through the plane ("Placing and routing decoupling capacitors").
Star grounding: joining returns at one point to keep large currents away from a sensitive reference ("Star grounding").
Stitching vias: vias that tie ground layers and copper fills together ("Ground stitching vias").
A microcontroller pin's current jumps 100 milliamps in 2 nanoseconds. A 100 nanofarads capacitor with 1.
5 nanohenries of loop inductance lets the supply dip by L change in I over change in t equals 1. 5 nanohenries times 0. 1 amps over 2 nanoseconds equals 75 millivolts.
The same capacitor with its ground via 5 mm away has 6. 5 nanohenries, and the dip is 325 millivolts. A 3. 3 volts supply with a 5% window allows only ±165 millivolts.
Moving the via to the pad fixes it. That is the whole idea.
"I give return currents a short, well-defined path.

A solid ground plane right next to the signal layers, never cut by slots; a via at every ground pad, placed right at the pad; the shortest possible loop for decoupling capacitors, since each millimetre of trace is about a nanohenry; separate noisy and sensitive returns by placement rather than by cutting the plane; a star point only where I need one; and stitching vias so no ground pour is floating.
The goal is small loops and no shared impedance between circuits."
Quick check. Where should the ground via for a decoupling capacitor be placed?
